extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society, natural philosophers and practicing scientists of the 17th century (readers of Philosophical Transactions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for writing and publishing experimental and observational reports in natural philosophy: describing apparatus, recording measurements, stating aims, and defending theoretical claims with argument and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe experimental apparatus and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a full description of the instruments used (shape, dimensions, valves, neck size, etc.) and the way they were employed (how lowered, orientation, how measurements were taken).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes a glass bottle with a brass ring and inward-opening flap, and a two-foot glass cylinder drawn out at one end; includes how they were let down, oriented (mouth downwards, crooked end uppermost), and measured (compass, measuring from bottom to hole). Include figures/plates when helpful (e.g., fig. 1. pl. 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform repeated trials and confirm results with independent instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat experiments multiple times and, where possible, corroborate findings using different instruments or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The compression-of-air result was confirmed by repeated trials and by using two different instruments which produced the same proportions at various depths; authors explicitly state repeated experiments confirmed the finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify measurements precisely and report units and numerical values
rubrics_metrics.description: Report numeric measurements (depths, weights, magnitudes, angular distances) and the units used to allow others to evaluate and reproduce the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: depth stated as 33 feet; weight proportions (salt to fresh water as 42 to 41); angular separations given in degrees, minutes and seconds (e.g., 20° 55' 20''); magnitudes tracked (third, fourth, fifth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use weighing and careful measurement to infer quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, determine quantities indirectly by weighing and comparative measurement rather than relying on casual observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The compression of air was determined by weighing the bottle in several states (half full, full, emptied) and deducing the quantity of displaced air from weight differences; a bottle with a very small neck was used to detect single drops when measuring water densities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare results across conditions and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Report and compare measurements under different conditions (e.g., depths, salt vs fresh water) to contextualize the findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportions were reported 'at that depth' and 'proportionably at other depths'; the weight of salt water compared to fresh water was measured and reported to show effect on experiments and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain practical applicability and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: State how experimental results can be applied or what practical problems they help solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors explicitly note the usefulness of the air-compression experiments for divers (knowing to what depth they can endure compression and how to supply air in vessels for diving bells).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide dates, observer names, and precise timestamps for observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the dates of observations and credit observers, so temporal behavior and provenance can be assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Astronomical observations list exact dates (e.g., April 29, June 20, July 3, etc.) and observers (Mr. Picard, Don Anthelme, M. Cassini, Hevelius), enabling tracking of appearance and disappearance over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record celestial coordinates and angular separations
rubrics_metrics.description: For astronomical reports, give coordinates (longitude, right ascension, declination/latitude) and measured angular distances from fixed stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new star's longitude, right ascension, north latitude, declination and distances from neighboring stars are listed (e.g., longitude 1° 55' of Aquarius; right ascension 293° 33'; distances such as 17° 47' 50''), facilitating identification and comparison with catalogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track temporal changes in observed phenomena (magnitude/time series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report changes in brightness, size or other observable properties across dated observations to reveal dynamics or periodicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new star is followed across months with magnitude assessments (third, fourth, fifth magnitude) and noted increases and decreases on specific dates; commentators infer possible recurrence periods from these records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate instruments for microscopic observations and taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: For small organisms or fine morphological features, use microscopes and record distinguishing characters (coloration, spots, wing patterns), and provide taxonomic naming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The insect hatched from kermes is described in macroscopic terms but the text advises referral 'to the testimony of a microscope' for features like stings and head balls; a Latin descriptive name is proposed based on morphology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support theoretical claims with argumentation and by addressing objections
rubrics_metrics.description: When making theoretical assertions, accompany them with arguments, answer likely objections, and show how the theory explains observed phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borelli 'brings arguments; answers objections and difficulties' and solves many phenomena; the review criticises Hobbes for 'obstacity' and 'ignorance in mathematics' and praises responses that refute false reasonings. Authors are commended when they show how their principles resolve general problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure dissertations and treatises with clear divisions stating problems and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay out the work's aims and divide it into parts each with a stated objective (e.g., general problem, resolution, particular examples, implications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steno's Prodromus is said to be divided into four parts with explicit purposes (showing the question is useful, resolving the general problem, examining particular solids, and representing different states and explaining phenomena like the deluge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground medical and physiological claims in anatomy, observation, and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical dissertations should derive mechanisms from anatomical structure, include observations/experiments, and propose remedies based on physiological reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower's dissertation on the heart and catarrh is praised for observations and experiments and for deriving the origin of rheums from serum of the blood, then proposing cures by withdrawing that pabulum or precipitating serosity via kidneys or pores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid baseless conjecture; require accurate observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticize and avoid works that rely on 'absurd conjectures' without sufficient evidence; demand accurate observations to establish doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review condemns dissertations 'filled with absurd conjectures and reasonings' about pestilential contagion and urges many accurate observations to clear obscure doctrines (e.g., on tainted air and its bodily effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: When editing or translating classical works, include original text, credible manuscripts, and scholarly commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce editions that provide original languages, reliable manuscripts, translations, and annotations/commentaries to make the work useful to scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diophantus is printed in Greek and Latin with Bachet's commentaries and Fermat's annotations and private letters; the Arabic-to-Latin translation of Philosophus Autodidactus is printed in both languages with a preface and learned apparatus.
